#### AI for Complex Data 

## About us 

 Lium is an AI platform that helps teams get reliable answers from large, complex, multimodal datasets. It was built for the kind of data work that traditional AI tools cannot handle: scientific measurements, sensor streams, geospatial imagery, seismic surveys, engineering models, technical documents, instrument outputs, proprietary files, and other messy datasets from the physical world. These datasets power critical work in advanced industries like energy, climate, infrastructure, space, geoscience, engineering, and scientific research, but they are often too large, fragmented, or domain-specific for generic AI systems to reason over reliably. Lium gives experts a direct way to work with that data. Scientists, engineers, operators, analysts, and subject matter experts can describe what they want to learn in natural language, and Lium handles the technical work behind the scenes: connecting disparate data sources, processing terabyte-scale workloads, provisioning compute as needed, building reusable analysis tools, running tests, and producing knowledge artifacts that experts can inspect and validate. Instead of waiting on custom pipelines or rebuilding scripts for every new question, teams can move from raw data to useful answers in a matter of minutes. This means anyone in an organization can ask what they want of their data without infrastructure, scale, or software complexity standing in the way. And when an analysis is validated, it does not disappear into a notebook or one-off report. It becomes a reusable capability that the rest of the organization can run, trust, and build on. For teams working on high-stakes problems in the physical world, Lium makes large, complex data usable. It turns raw information into trusted answers, repeatable workflows, and organizational knowledge that compounds with every project.

Marieke van Hout - de Groot 2mo Edited What if you could just ask? OpendTect is powerful—but finding the right tool, setting up a workflow, or figuring out what to do next isn't always straightforward. So, what if you could simply ask? At IMAGE 2026, 17–20 August, we'll be giving a first look at something new we're working on: an AI chatbot designed to help you with your OpendTect workflows. The idea is simple: make it easier to get from a geoscience question to the tools and workflows you need, with AI assistance directly supporting the way you work in OpendTect. And that's not the only thing cooking. We'll showcase AI well-log conditioning using an agentic workflow powered by Lium. The workflow reads your LAS files directly—no OpendTect or import/export step is needed to get started. Instead of manually inspecting, editing and conditioning logs, the agent analyzes the LAS file and generates both the conditioned results and a report within minutes. Once you're happy with the conditioning workflow, you can save it and apply the same filtering and conditioning in bulk across your other LAS files. Or, if you prefer, each LAS file can be analyzed and treated individually. You decide how much to automate—the user remains in control. The resulting conditioned logs can then be written to new LAS files, ready for use in OpendTect or elsewhere. During the demo, we'll take the workflow all the way through and show the final conditioned logs in OpendTect. Lium encompasses all data types supported in an OpendTect project, and at IMAGE you'll get the chance to experiment with it using your own prompts. We'll also be demonstrating our new semi-automated fault picker, combining automation with interactive interpretation so that the geoscientist remains in control of the result. For us, these are exciting examples of how AI can become a practical part of everyday geoscience workflows—helping you work more efficiently while making sophisticated interpretation tools easier to access and use. We'll be demonstrating all three at IMAGE 2026, and this time we don't just want you to watch. Bring your questions. Try your own prompts. If you could ask OpendTect one question, what would it be? dGB Earth Sciences #OpendTect #AI #LLM #seismic #geology #geophysics Like Comment Share Lium 342 followers 2mo Edited Report this post What multimodal AI actually means... Everyone says multimodal AI means it can read text and look at a picture. Sure, but that's just scratching the surface. Let’s say a geologist has a SEG-Y file (seismic data), an LAS file (well log), and a folder of TIFFs (core photos), all for the same well. The question isn't whether an AI can open all three. It's whether it can tell you what they say about the same exact spot underground. Most tools can't. They squash everything into one internal format before reasoning over it, which works fine for a photo and a caption, but doesn't work for seismic data where the whole point is exact numbers. Try uploading a SEG-Y file to ChatGPT, it won't even recognize it, and you'll hit a size limit before getting through a real dataset anyway. So instead of converting anything, keep the files as they are. SEG-Y stays SEG-Y. Anchor them to one point, a well, a location, whatever, and pull the actual value from each file at that spot. Ask about the well, get the seismic reading, the log, and the core photo, straight from source. No guessing involved. More details in the comments. 1 Comment Like Comment Share Lium 342 followers 2mo Report this post Most AI tools can't actually ingest satellite telemetry in its native format. It’s not that they can’t analyze the file, they literally cannot open the file. A single LEO satellite puts out multiple gigabytes of telemetry a day, and a full constellation is generating terabytes daily on top of years of accumulated archives from missions that are still running. CCSDS packets and IRIG 106 Chapter 10 files are not something you can drag into ChatGPT. And a good chunk of what ground teams actually get isn't live anyway, it's been sitting onboard waiting for playback, so by the time anyone's looking at it the moment has already passed. The costly part is usually the correlation, not any single reading. A temperature value on its own rarely tells you much. That same value alongside a power spike and a thruster firing event is a different signal entirely, and most dashboards aren't built to show it that way. They present channels one at a time, which means the combination that actually mattered often goes unnoticed until later. How is your team currently handling this? Manual review, exception reports, or something you've built in-house? More detail on our approach is in the comments. 1 Comment Like Comment Share Lium 342 followers 2mo Report this post Every large telescope mission archives data with its own formats, naming conventions, and specialized tools. That makes analyzing data across surveys unnecessarily difficult. That’s a problem the Multimodal Universe project just solved. The project, led out of the Center for Astrophysics | Harvard & Smithsonian , standardized more than 80TB of observations, including radio and X-ray observations, stellar and galactic spectra, and variable-star light curves Previously, working across these surveys meant learning how to access, process, and align each dataset separately. Now, researchers have one dataset where they can work across them using the same tools and formats, even from a laptop. CfA researcher Mike Smith , who leads the project, put it simply: nobody should need a PhD in a specific survey's archival system just to load its data and start working with it. Mike's work is supported by Lium and open source for anyone to use. We are happy to further contribute to the community by making the archive available in Lium, pre-connected and ready for natural language analysis. Create a free account and try it here: http://bit.ly/4g2iVr4 Read the full story on Multimodal Universe here: https://lnkd.in/gnVbYrvJ Like Comment Share Lium 342 followers 2mo Report this post A well log from 1987. A seismic survey from last year. Technically both count as "subsurface data," but that's about where the similarity ends. The 1987 log is probably LAS, hand-typed off a logging tool that hasn't existed in decades. Or DLIS, which is worse. The seismic survey is SEG-Y, a binary format built in the 1970s for magnetic tape that's still hauling around gigabytes to terabytes of trace data indexed by shot point. Core samples got logged in a field notebook, or a spreadsheet, or an image scan, depending on who was on site that week. Production history sits in a separate operational database. SEG-Y wasn't written with LAS in mind. LAS wasn't written with a production database in mind. Each format solved a narrow problem for one tool at one point in time. Reservoir characterization means a geoscientist making all of them cooperate anyway, porosity and permeability and saturation pulled out of files that were never on the same page. Most of that pulling still happens by hand. Someone opens each file individually, in whatever proprietary viewer it demands, then stitches the results together in a doc or a spreadsheet before anyone else on the team can see them. Lium puts LAS, DLIS, SEG-Y, and everything else in one AI workspace, so the formats stop being the obstacle. The analysis is shareable from the start, not reconstructed after the fact for whoever asks next. Read the full article here: https://lnkd.in/g8EqrDec Like Comment Share Lium 342 followers 2mo Report this post NOAA puts out 20 terabytes of environmental data every day. Free. Public. Critical to energy, insurance, agriculture, shipping. Most of it never gets used in time. Here's why. An energy trader needs a 72-hour wind forecast. It's sitting in a GRIB2 file, no index, encoded values that need a lookup table just to read. An insurer needs flood exposure across a portfolio during an active hurricane. That means manually overlaying NetCDF storm surge grids against policy locations. Hours of work in a window measured in minutes. HDF5 satellite data has the same problem in a different shape. Technically self-describing, but the metadata is scattered across the file. Pulling one variable takes multiple sequential reads through specialized libraries most teams don't have on hand. None of this is a data shortage. Energy, insurance, agriculture, and shipping are sitting on more relevant data than they've ever had access to. What they're short on is the layer that turns a GRIB2 file or an HDF5 archive into something a person can actually query in the middle of a decision. Pulling FEMA flood maps into a format that plays nice with the county's stormwater GIS layers. Converting NOAA precipitation data so it lines up with a client's decade of internal sensor readings. None of that is modeling. It's prep work, and it happens before the actual analysis even starts. Most AI tools skip past this problem entirely, because they assume the data is already clean and already yours to feed in as a PDF or CSV. Hydrology and water resources work rarely looks like that. It's shapefiles, NetCDF, raster layers, telemetry, all sitting in different systems, in different formats, updated on different schedules. Lium was built for that layer of the work specifically. It reads the formats water resources teams actually use, lines up datasets by coordinates or timestamps instead of requiring everything to be pre-converted, and lets someone ask a question in plain language once the data is aligned. The modeling still depends on the modeler. What's changing is how much of the week gets eaten before they even get to do it.
